draft.title: The real number system
card: Natural and integers
Natural numbers are the counting numbers \(1, 2, 3\) and so on. Integers add zero and the negative whole numbers, such as \(-4\).
Rational

A rational number can be written as a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) of two integers, with \(b \ne 0\). So \(-4\), \(\frac{3}{5}\) and \(0.25\) are rational. Every integer is rational, because \(-4 = \frac{-4}{1}\).
Irrational
An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of integers. Its decimal never ends and never repeats. Examples are \(\pi\) and \(\sqrt{2}\).
Real
Rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers. A number is never both. Roots such as \(\sqrt{9}\) are rational, because \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).
draft.remember: Natural numbers sit inside integers, inside rationals. Add the irrationals to get the reals.

a.q: Which number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers?
a.why: \(\sqrt{7}\) is not a whole number and its decimal never ends or repeats, so it cannot be a fraction of integers. \(\sqrt{16} = 4\) looks like a root but is rational. The other two are fractions of integers.
a.clue: Check which options are fractions of integers in disguise.

b.q: Which statement about the number \(-6\) is true?
opts: It is an integer and a rational number
It is a natural number and an integer
It is a rational number but not an integer
It is an integer but not a rational number
b.why: \(-6\) is a negative whole number, so it is an integer. It equals \(\frac{-6}{1}\), so it is also rational. It is not natural, because natural numbers are the counting numbers, which are positive.
b.clue: Every integer can be written over 1.

b.best: It is an integer and a rational number

problems.detail: "Roots such as \(\sqrt{9}\) are rational" can be read as saying roots in general are rational, which clashes with \(\sqrt{2}\) being irrational two lines earlier. It should say that some roots, such as \(\sqrt{9}\), are rational because they simplify to an integer.

check.summary: Both questions and explanations are correct. The card's line "Roots such as \(\sqrt{9}\) are rational" could suggest all roots are rational and should say "some roots".
